summary: Updates the 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery protocol of RFCs 6775 and 8505 with Address-Protected Neighbor Discovery, which protects the owner of an address against theft and impersonation in low-power and lossy networks. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: On a network of small sensors, one gadget could pretend to be another by claiming its address. This document adds a lock so that only the real owner of an address can use it.

questions: how to prevent address theft in 6lowpan
how does ap-nd prevent address theft
what is the ndp signature option
subtitle: Lets a low-power IPv6 device prove it owns an address, so no other node on the network can steal it.

tldr.problem: In 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery, address ownership is checked with a ROVR that can be derived from a spoofable EUI-64, so an attacker that knows the mapping can fake it, steal the address and redirect traffic.
tldr.mechanism: A node derives a Crypto-ID from a public key, places it in the ROVR field when registering, and answers a challenge from the 6LR with a signed Neighbor Solicitation carrying a nonce, a Crypto-ID Parameters Option and an NDP Signature Option.
tldr.outcome: Once an address is registered with a Crypto-ID and ownership is proved, only the owner can change the registration, which enforces source address validation. The RFC updates RFC 8505 and has been updated by RFC 9926 and RFC 9927.

facts.label: Recommended Crypto-ID size
facts.value: 128 bits (at least 64 bits for backward compatibility)

today: RFC 8928 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 8505. It has been updated by RFC 9926 and RFC 9927.

sections.title: The Address Theft Problem
sections.content:
6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery (RFC 6775) adapts IPv6 Neighbor Discovery to constrained Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs). A 6LoWPAN Node (6LN) registers its addresses with a 6LoWPAN Router (6LR), which relays the registration to the 6LoWPAN Border Router (6LBR), the central repository of registered addresses. The first node to register an address wins.

RFC 8505 adds a Registration Ownership Verifier (ROVR) to tie an address to its owner. The ROVR can be derived from a link-layer EUI-64, but an EUI-64 can be spoofed, so any node that knows the address-to-ROVR mapping could fake the ROVR, steal the address and redirect its traffic.

RFC 8928 closes this gap with Address-Protected Neighbor Discovery (AP-ND). The 6LN generates a cryptographic identifier, the Crypto-ID, and places it in the ROVR field. The 6LR validates ownership before it creates new registration state or changes existing information. The result gives the same conceptual benefit as Source Address Validation Improvement (RFC 7039), but it relies on state that the address owner installs and maintains rather than on snooping.

Unlike SEND (RFC 3971) with CGAs, the address itself is not derived from the keys. That keeps better 6LoWPAN compression possible for addresses based on L2 addresses.
sections.eli5: Right now the network only trusts whoever shouted an address first, and a clever gadget can copy another gadget's name tag. AP-ND adds a signature that only the real owner can write.

sections.title: How the Crypto-ID Fits In
sections.content:
The Crypto-ID is carried in the ROVR field of the EARO (and of the Extended Duplicate Address Request, EDAR) and is derived from a public key and additional parameters. Using it is the RECOMMENDED method for computing a ROVR. A node that has the needed cryptographic primitives SHOULD use a Crypto-ID by default, and a new C flag in the EARO says that the ROVR is a Crypto-ID and that the 6LN MAY be challenged for ownership.

To derive it, the hash function of the chosen signature scheme is applied to the Crypto-ID Parameters Option (CIPO), with all reserved and padding bits set to zero, and the leftmost bits of the result are used. A Crypto-ID size of 128 bits is RECOMMENDED, or at least 64 bits when backward compatibility with RFC 8505 is needed.

Three new things carry the proof: the CIPO holds the public key and parameters, the NDP Signature Option holds the signature, and a Nonce Option from RFC 3971 is used in the challenge. The scope is a 6LoWPAN LLN, typically a stub network connected through a 6LBR. The RFC mandates peer-wise L2 security between a host and its 6LR, and protection of all LLN links between the 6LR and the 6LBR so that a packet validated by the first 6LR can be safely routed on.
sections.eli5: The Crypto-ID is like a fingerprint made from your secret key. You put the fingerprint next to your address, and later you can prove it is really yours by signing something.

sections.title: The New Fields and Options
sections.content:
The Enhanced Address Registration Option (EARO, type 33) from RFC 8505 gains the C flag taken from its reserved bits. No new status codes are defined: the existing "Validation Requested" and "Validation Failed" are used.

The Crypto-ID Parameters Option (CIPO, type 39) has fields for the public key length, a Crypto-Type, an 8-bit Modifier, the length of the associated EARO, the public key itself and padding to an 8-byte boundary. The modifier lets a node form several Crypto-IDs from one key pair, which reduces traceability without requiring many key pairs.

The NDP Signature Option (NDPSO, type 40) carries the digital signature and padding. Unlike the RSA Signature Option of SEND, it has no key hash field. Instead the leftmost 128 bits of the ROVR in the EARO are used to find the matching CIPO, which may be in the same message or in a table built by an earlier one. It signs a fixed set of fields rather than all earlier options. A message with an NDPSO MUST contain exactly one EARO whose ROVR is a Crypto-ID tied to the signing key.

A new A flag in the 6LoWPAN Capability Indication Option says that AP-ND is globally activated in the network. The 6LBR sets it and the 6LRs propagate it, typically once all 6LRs have been migrated.
sections.eli5: There are two new forms to fill in. One lists your public key, and the other holds your signature. A small tick box tells everyone that the name tag is a fingerprint, so they should ask for proof.

sections.title: The Challenge and Response Flow
sections.content:
A 6LN registers with a 6LR one hop away using an NS with an EARO whose C flag is set. If the 6LR has no consistent state for this node, it MUST challenge with an NA(EARO) carrying the status "Validation Requested" (5) and a Nonce Option. The 6LN SHOULD then retry with an NS that holds the EARO, the CIPO, its own nonce and the NDPSO. Both nonces are covered by the signature, which gives contributory behavior and better security even if one party generates its nonce poorly.

The 6LR rebuilds the Crypto-ID from the CIPO, checks that it matches the ROVR, and verifies the signature. If that works, it passes the registration to the 6LBR in an EDAR/EDAC exchange. Otherwise it answers "Validation Failed" (10), and the node SHOULD try another Crypto-Type. On later revalidation with the same 6LR, the node MAY omit the CIPO to save bandwidth.

When the A flag is set, the 6LR MUST challenge a node before creating a binding with the C flag set, and also when a new registration tries to change a parameter of a validated binding, such as its source link-layer address. A valid registration MUST NOT be altered until a challenge is complete. The 6LBR trusts the 6LR to perform the verification, because the 6LR and 6LBR are assumed to have a security association protecting the EDAR and EDAC messages. If the 6LR does not support the Crypto-Type, it MUST reply with status 10 and no challenge.
sections.eli5: When a new gadget says "this address is mine", the router replies with a random number and says "prove it". The gadget signs that number along with its own, and the router checks the signature. A copycat has no key, so it fails.

sections.title: Signature Schemes and Signing
sections.content:
Cryptographic agility comes from the Crypto-Type field. Three schemes are defined, as the registered Crypto-Types 0 to 2.

  • ECDSA256 (type 0): ECDSA with the NIST P-256 curve and SHA-256. It MUST be supported by all implementations.
  • Ed25519 (type 1): PureEdDSA over Edwards25519 with SHA-512. It MAY be supported.
  • ECDSA25519 (type 2): ECDSA over the Weierstrass form Wei25519 with SHA-256. It MAY also be supported.

Sharing SHA-256 between two of the schemes helps constrained devices that cannot afford several hash implementations in program memory.

The signed message is the concatenation of a 128-bit Message Type tag, the CIPO, the 16-byte Target Address, the NonceLR, the NonceLN and the 1-byte option length of the EARO. The 6LR first checks that the EARO Length in the CIPO matches the EARO, regenerates the Crypto-ID from the CIPO, and only then verifies the signature with the public key in the CIPO. The nonce is at least 6 bytes long, as defined in RFC 3971.
sections.eli5: There are three secret-stamp styles, and every router must know the first one. The signature covers both random numbers and the address, so an old signature can't be reused.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Protection only works fully when every 6LR is upgraded. In a mixed network an attacker could attach to a legacy 6LR and fool the 6LBR, even if the A flag is already set. If a 6LR is compromised and knows the ROVR of the real owner, it could pretend the owner has moved to it and passed validation, and then attract traffic or let an attacker take the address.

Nonces should never repeat but do not need to be unpredictable. A rogue node can still try a denial of service by registering many addresses, so a 6LR MUST protect itself and reject excess registrations with status 2 "Neighbor Cache Full". The 64-bit minimum Crypto-ID gives a collision chance of 0.01% for a network of 66 million nodes, and nodes are RECOMMENDED not to derive the registered address from the ROVR.

Key handling rules are strict. The same private key MUST NOT be reused with more than one signature scheme instantiation or for anything other than NDPSO signatures. Each ECDSA signing operation MUST use a fresh random ephemeral key, which rules out deterministic ECDSA. Public keys in the CIPO must be fully validated. Using different modifiers per address improves privacy but makes the 6LR store several CIPOs with the same key.
sections.eli5: The lock only works if every router has the new lock. Keep your secret stamp to yourself and use a fresh random number each time you sign, or a snoop could work out your stamp.
